Adult Blunt-snouted mullet attain a maximum recorded total length of 21.9 centimeters [Li = 21.9 centimeters], a value that positions them as moderate-sized members of the family Mullidae. Males and females converge on this upper size limit, though females tend to display slightly heavier bodies at equivalent lengths. The ultimate body mass for mature females reaches approximately 112 grams [Wwi = approximately 112 grams], derived from the robust length-weight relationship observed in the species. Juveniles and sub-adults, by contrast, show substantially lower mass values. At the onset of sexual maturity, individuals weigh roughly 11.6 grams [Wwp = roughly 11.6 grams], reflecting the considerable somatic investment required before gonadal activity commences. This transition from the immature, pre-reproductive stage to a reproductive adult involves a nearly tenfold increase in mass, underscoring the energetic demands of growth in a temperate marine environment. Studies based on otolith microstructure have confirmed that these size benchmarks are consistently achieved across the species range, with only minor regional variations linked to local prey abundance and thermal regimes.

The timing of reproductive maturity in Blunt-snouted mullet is linked directly to body size, with puberty occurring when individuals reach a total length of 10.5 centimeters [Lp = 10.5 centimeters]. This length at puberty represents a threshold below which gonadal recrudescence is rarely observed, a pattern consistent with the size-dependent maturation schedules common among iteroparous teleosts. Reaching this threshold typically requires the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to sustain both gamete production and continued somatic growth. In the Mediterranean populations where this species has been most intensively studied, the length at which 50% of individuals are mature aligns closely with this value. The consistency of this metric across different sampling years and locations suggests a robust, genetically canalized response to environmental cues, rather than a highly plastic trait. Further work examining the relationship between local productivity and age at first reproduction would help clarify the extent to which this length threshold can be modulated by ecological context.

Reproductive output in Blunt-snouted mullet is substantial, with females producing a maximum of approximately 4,384 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4,384 eggs per day] when water temperatures reach 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C]. This daily fecundity estimate, derived from work on the closely related Mullus barbatus, reflects the potential for very high egg production during a single daily spawning event. Such a prolific output is characteristic of broadcast spawners that release pelagic eggs into an unpredictable planktonic environment, where mortality rates are notoriously high. The estimate is based on a thermal regime typical of early spring conditions in the species core distribution. Whether this maximum rate is sustained throughout the entire spawning season or is confined to a relatively brief peak period remains uncertain, as field sampling of gonadosomatic indices suggests considerable within-season variation. Future studies employing daily egg counts from captive females held under controlled thermal conditions could resolve this temporal pattern more definitively.

The fertilised ova of Blunt-snouted mullet are pelagic and remarkably small, each weighing just 0.000065 grams [Wwb = 0.000065 grams] based on an average egg diameter of half a millimeter. This extremely low weight per egg is typical of marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, yolk-poor eggs as part of a high-fecundity, low-investment reproductive strategy. The chorionate embryo develops within a transparent, spherical capsule that offers minimal physical protection but facilitates rapid diffusion of oxygen and metabolic waste. Following fertilisation, the cleavage-stage embryo progresses through a rapid series of mitotic divisions, with the blastula-stage embryo forming within hours. Given the small size of the egg, the resulting yolk-sac larva emerges at a correspondingly diminutive size, entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves. The trade-off between egg size and fecundity is stark in this species: the investment in each individual offspring is minimal, allowing for the production of tens of thousands of eggs over a single spawning season, a strategy that presumably buffers against high larval mortality in the pelagic environment.

Maximum longevity in Blunt-snouted mullet has been estimated at 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days], based on recapture data and otolith readings from wild populations maintained at an average annual temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This duration is comparatively long for a mullid of its size, suggesting a relatively slow pace of life that may be linked to the modest metabolic demands of life on the continental shelf. The thermal conditions under which this longevity was recorded correspond closely to the summer means in the species core Mediterranean habitat, where water temperatures regularly reach 21 °C. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in reproductive output and a slowing of annual growth increments, as visible in the narrowing of otolith annuli. The oldest recorded fish in any population typically show evidence of compromised swim bladder function and reduced feeding efficiency, likely contributing to natural mortality. Whether populations inhabiting cooler, deeper waters achieve even greater ages remains an open question, as sampling effort has been concentrated in shallower, warmer areas.
